item.title: Stargazing - Near Total Lunar Eclipse — Thu Aug 27, 10:30 PM — None
item.description:
Join the Stargazing Devils to watch an exceptional lunar eclipse at midnight (12 AM) on the night of Aug. 27th. The Full Moon will slip through Earth's shadow, resulting in a partial lunar eclipse. It will be visible from much of North and South America and parts of Europe and Africa. At maximum eclipse, about 93% of the Moon's diameter will be inside Earth's dark central shadow, called the umbra. The Moon will not be completely covered, but it can look dramatically darkened, with a rusty, coppery tint along the covered edge.
Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch with just your eyes. Binoculars or a small telescope can give you a closer view of Earth's curved shadow moving across the Moon. Source - NASA

Source: Duke University

item.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star (Theatre for the Very Young) — Sun Aug 30, 10:00 AM — Raleigh Little Theatre
item.description:
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is an interactive children’s theatre piece for very young audiences, performed by two Star Keepers named Glimmer and Sparkle. It’s time for the night sky to fill with stars, but one important star — Little Star, the wishing star — is missing because Sparkle rushed through putting the stars away the previous morning and muddled everything up. What follows is a search-and-rescue adventure as the two star keepers (and the audience) hunt for Little Star, discovering along the way that all the other stars have been put in the wrong places too and need to be moved to their proper place. Audience members help the Star Keepers find and re-organize the sky just in time for nightfall so that everyone can make a wish on their favorite star. Twinkle, Twinkle explores the ideas that mistakes happen, feelings are valid, and no one has to face hard things alone – all wrapped up in a genuinely joyful romp about stars.
By Ernie Nolan Produced by special arrangemen

item.title: NIH Common Forms Requirements: Biosketch and Current and Pending (Other) Support — Tue Sep 1, 11:00 AM
item.description:
This session provides an overview of changes to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) grant application requirements, including new Common Forms that will be required for due dates on or after January 25, 2026.

item.title: Constitution Day: Panel Discussion on the Constitution and Executive Power — Mon Sep 14, 5:30 PM — The Sonja Haynes Stone Center for Research in Black Culture and History
item.description:
When the thirteen colonies declared independence, the new United States of America faced a central question: how could it create a strong executive without a king? In honor of Constitution Day, the Program for Public Discourse and the UNC School of Law will host a panel discussion on the U.S. Constitution and executive power. Moderated by Suzanne Globetti (UNC), Michael Gerhardt (UNC) and Saikrishna Prakash (UVA) will discuss the powers the Constitution granted the president and what they mean today.
September 17 is Constitution Day and Citizenship Day (Constitution Day). This day commemorates the September 17, 1787 signing of the U.S. Constitution.
Students who attend in person can earn CLE credit. No tickets are necessary; seating is first-come, first-served. Reserved tickets are available for guests traveling from outside Chapel Hill. Please email publicdiscourse@unc.edu to reserve seats. We will serve pizza after the event.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: “She Will Be Quite a Manager”: From Plantation Owner to Girl Boss — Thu Sep 17, 5:30 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: What do a Civil War-era plantation owner and a modern “girl boss” have in common? More than you think. Adelicia Acklen and Dorothy Thomas were two of the most powerful plantation-owning women—one in the US South and the other in South America—but both wielded the power of ownership by deploying and playing on particular ideas of femininity. This talk hosted by Carolina Public Humanities traces their unsettling legacy into the present, asking what happens when women gain power within systems built on inequality. Free, but space is limited; registration is required via the Carolina Public Humanities event webpage. About the speaker: Tanya Shields is an Associate Professor of Women’s and Gender Studies whose research focuses on Caribbean studies and plantation logics. She teaches courses on the Caribbean, the arts of activism, growing up girls globally, and the continuing influence of plantation economics and politics. item.title: Dr. Dave Fossum | UNC Music Research Forum — Fri Sep 25, 3:30 PM — Person Hall
item.description: Dr. Dave Fossum, Arizona State University, National Humanities Center “What’s an Arrangement Worth?: Copyright, Folk Music, and the Value of Creativity in Turkey” Copyright is supposed to reward creators for their creativity. Yet there are no clear criteria for measuring the value of this creativity or how creative a work is. Drawing on a case study from my book, Copyright Consciousness, this talk links implicit criteria of creative value to a larger history of nation-building. The launching point for my inquiry is a policy of Turkey’s copyright collecting societies, who long offered arrangers of public domain folk music only a (10%) royalty on their arrangements (whereas a 100% royalty is common in most jurisdictions). While some arrangers complained about this policy, my ethnographic data reveal that many musicians found it natural. This workshop is offered by the University Libraries Health Sciences Library and led by Emma Barrett-Catton. It is part of the Systematic Review Methods and Advancing Clinical Research Skills workshop tracks.

As a young woman, Lanah Sawyer had a rare kind of courage. Only seventeen, a stepchild in a working family, she was easy to dismiss as a mere “sewing girl.” Yet, when an affluent gentleman showed an interest in her, she dared to image that he might really be interested in her. Violently, he dashed that dream—leaving her disoriented, distressed, and unmoored. Then, she gathered her courage and did what no one else in the nation’s biggest city had done in half a century

item.title: Leveraging Generative AI for Research Tasks (Research Week Event) — Thu Oct 22, 2:00 PM
item.description:
Want to know how generative AI (GenAI) can be used to support your research? This workshop covers various GenAI tools that have applications for research tasks including tools that support writing manuscripts, exploring and summarizing literature (e.g., Research Rabbit, Consensus, and Undermind), performing data analysis (e.g., Julius and ProQuest TDM Studio), and conducting evidence syntheses (including systematic and scoping reviews). An overview of library resources that support GenAI including PromptLab and the Library AI Studio is also provided.
This workshop is intended for those with some existing knowledge of genAI. If you need more of an introduction to AI, please check out the Library's other AI-related workshops.
This workshop is offered by the UNC Health Sciences Library and led by Luke Barron. It is part of the For Researchers and Advancing Clinical Research Skills workshop tracks.
